disclaimer: RESEARCH AID, NOT LEGAL ADVICE. Compiled by an automated research process on the retrieval date and not reviewed by a lawyer. Laws, regulations and regulator positions change; every entry must be confirmed by qualified counsel before it is relied on to configure a production website. Where a source was silent or unclear the registry records null/unclear rather than inferring a requirement, and absence of an entry is not evidence that no requirement exists.

how_to_read.required_website_behavior: Only behavior traced to a cited statute, binding regulation or court ruling (basis = statute | regulation | case_law). Each applies only to a business the law covers; see laws[].applicability.
how_to_read.regulator_guidance: Official but non-binding regulator statements. Not requirements.
how_to_read.recommended_conservative_practices: Recommendations authored for this registry (basis = recommendation_not_statutory). Never cite these as legal requirements.
how_to_read.null_values: null = unclear, silent, or not verified. It never means 'not required'.
how_to_read.confidence: high = text read from an official source; medium/low = partial read, summarised extract, secondary source or interpretive step.
how_to_read.customer_override: Per-jurisdiction slot for a client decision. Set active=true with reason, approved_by, approved_date. treat_as_applicable=false (client says the law does not cover them) and any behavior_overrides entry that relaxes a required behavior should carry a counsel_reference. Overrides are stored by consumers of the registry; the shipped registry always has active=false.

scope_and_gaps: U.S. federal law (COPPA, FTC Act s.5, HIPAA, GLBA, VPPA, wiretap/CIPA-style litigation risk) was not researched.
State children's/teen design-code, biometric (e.g. Illinois BIPA), data-broker and breach laws were not researched except where noted in a record.
EU member-state implementations of ePrivacy art. 5(3) and national regulator guidance (e.g. CNIL, TDDDG) were not researched; the EU record is the EU-level baseline only.
Australia and Japan were not researched (no official source could be read); other countries are out of scope.
For states with no comprehensive law identified, absence was mostly confirmed from secondary trackers, not from each legislature's site.
Applicability thresholds are reproduced from the cited text; whether a specific business meets them is a factual and legal question for the client and counsel.

conservative_practices.practice: Do not assume a client is below a statutory threshold or exempt. Have the client (with counsel) confirm applicability per jurisdiction and record the decision in customer_override; until confirmed, configure the site as if the law applies.

Treat a Global Privacy Control signal (Sec-GPC: 1 / navigator.globalPrivacyControl) from any U.S. visitor as a valid opt-out of sale, sharing and targeted advertising, including in states whose statute is silent, permissive or not yet effective.
Show a persistent footer link to an opt-out / privacy-choices control on every page for all U.S. visitors, separate from the cookie banner and from the privacy policy text.
Link the privacy notice from the home page (and site footer) with link text that contains the word "privacy", and show a last-updated date in the notice.
Make declining or opting out as easy and as prominent as accepting; no pre-ticked boxes, no consent inferred from scrolling or continued browsing.
Where prior consent is required, or where the visitor's location cannot be determined reliably, do not set or read non-essential cookies or fire analytics/advertising tags until the visitor opts in.

On pages that reveal health, precise location, children's or other sensitive information, do not load advertising or third-party tracking technology without opt-in consent, regardless of the visitor's state.

In jurisdictions with no comprehensive law identified, still apply the U.S. opt-out baseline (privacy notice link, opt-out control, GPC honored) rather than no controls; federal and sectoral law was not researched.
For laws enacted but not yet effective, apply the future requirements now rather than on the effective date.
Keep a record of the consent or opt-out state applied, the signal detected and the registry version in force, and show the visitor that an opt-out signal was honored.
Re-verify this registry against the cited sources at least quarterly and before each 1 January and 1 July, when most state amendments take effect.

researcher_notes.us-d: PART 2 LANDSCAPE (most important): the lead's 20-state list is stale. Four additional comprehensive laws were enacted in 2026 and have full records here: Oklahoma SB 546 (approved 2026-03-20, effective 2027-01-01; confirmed on oklegislature.gov), Alabama HB 351 'Alabama Personal Data Protection Act' (reported signed 2026-04-16/17, effective 2027-05-01; enrolled text read from the Alabama Legislature but signature NOT confirmed on an official page), Louisiana SB 386 / Act 502 'Louisiana Data Privacy Act' (signed 2026-05-29, effective 2027-01-01; confirmed on legis.la.gov), Vermont S.71 / Act 145 'Vermont Data Privacy and Online Surveillance Act' (signed 2026-06-16, effective 2028-01-01; confirmed on legislature.vermont.gov). Signal duties among these: Vermont = express opt-out preference signal duty; Louisiana = Texas-style authorized-agent/browser-setting duty with exceptions; Alabama = ambiguous (signal referenced, no express duty); Oklahoma = none. Indiana, Kentucky, Rhode Island = none found. Alabama and Vermont require a conspicuous opt-out link on the website; Vermont requires a home-page hyperlink containing the word 'privacy'; Louisiana prescribes exact 'NOTICE: We may sell your sensitive personal data.' wording. Kentucky HB 692 (2026) is recorded in US-KY. FEDERAL: no enacted federal comprehensive privacy law found. The SECURE Data Act (reported as H.R. 8413, 119th Congress; House Energy & Commerce Republican draft released 2026-04-22; subcommittee hearing 2026-06-03) would broadly preempt state privacy laws but, per the latest reporting found, had not been marked up or passed; congress.gov returned 403 so status is from secondary sources (StateScoop, law-firm alerts) only - re-check. Bus. Law 899-aa/899-bb) and the New York Child Data Protection Act (Gen. Bus. Law art. 39-FF, effective 2025-06-20) apply - not researched, dates from prior knowledge. amendments.description: CPRA (Proposition 24) amendments: added 'sharing' (cross-context behavioral advertising) opt-out, right to limit use of sensitive personal information, created the CPPA. Operative 2023-01-01; statute text states enforcement of CPRA-added provisions 'shall not commence until July 1, 2023'.
CPI adjustment of monetary thresholds: revenue threshold in 1798.140(d)(1)(A) raised from $25,000,000 to $26,625,000. Next statutory adjustment date is 2027-01-01 (odd-numbered years).

Neural data added to 'sensitive personal information' (1798.140(ae)(1)(G)). Present in the statute text effective 2026-01-01; the amending bill and its exact effective date were not separately verified.

CPPA regulation package (CCPA updates, cybersecurity audits, risk assessments, ADMT, insurance) approved by OAL 2025-09-22, effective 2026-01-01. Among website-relevant changes in the consolidated text: 7025(c)(6) now says a business 'must display' whether it processed the opt-out preference signal; 7026(g) requires a means to confirm an opt-out was processed.

AB 566 (California Opt Me Out Act), signed 2025-10-08, adds Civ. Code 1798.136: businesses that develop or maintain a browser must include a consumer-configurable setting that sends an opt-out preference signal. Regulates browser makers, not websites. Operative 2027-01-01.

applicability.summary: For-profit entity doing business in California that collects consumers' personal information, determines purposes and means of processing, and meets at least one of three thresholds.

thresholds.description: Annual gross revenues over $25,000,000 in the preceding calendar year as adjusted for CPI; adjusted figure is $26,625,000 effective 2025-01-01.
Alone or in combination, annually buys, sells, or shares the personal information of 100,000 or more consumers or households.
Derives 50 percent or more of annual revenues from selling or sharing consumers' personal information.

key_exemptions: Entities not organized or operated for profit are outside the 'business' definition (1798.140(d)(1)); AG page says the CCPA generally does not apply to nonprofits or government agencies
Other statutory exemptions (e.g. 1798.145) were not reviewed in this session

universal_opt_out.quote: Even if the business posts the above-referenced links, the business must still process opt-out preference signals
universal_opt_out.notes: Statute 1798.135(b)(3) reads as letting a business 'elect' between links (a) and signal (b); regulation 7025(e) interprets it as: signals must always be processed, the election is only whether to process them frictionlessly and drop the links. Neither statute nor regulation names GPC; 7025(b) sets format-neutral criteria (commonly used format such as HTTP header field or JavaScript object). The AG's consumer page and the 2022 Sephora release name GPC. effective_date is the CPRA operative date; the AG treated user-enabled global privacy controls as valid opt-outs under the earlier AG regulations (Sephora, 2022), whose text was not fetched. The 'targeted_advertising' and 'profiling' opt-out fields are null because the CCPA uses 'sharing' for cross-context behavioral advertising and handles ADMT via 2026 regulations not reviewed in detail here.

laws.cure_period: No general statutory cure period for administrative/AG enforcement now; the Sephora release refers to a '30-day period currently allowed' in 2022. The statute lets the CPPA consider whether to give time to cure (1798.199.45 area) and retains a 30-day cure for the data-breach private action (1798.150(b)). The date the AG 30-day cure ended (reported as 2023-01-01) was not pinpoint-verified.
laws.enforcer: California Privacy Protection Agency (administrative) and California Attorney General (civil)
laws.private_right_of_action: Limited to certain data breaches (Civ. Code 1798.150); not for website notice/opt-out violations.

laws.sensitive_data_notes: § 14-4707(a)(1): may not collect, process, or share sensitive data except where strictly necessary to provide or maintain a specific product or service requested by the consumer (consent is NOT an alternative basis in the text). § 14-4707(a)(2): may not 'Sell sensitive data' (no consent exception).

universal_opt_out.quote: A controller may utilize the following methods ... (i) Providing a clear and conspicuous link ... or (ii) On or before October 1, 2025, allowing a consumer to opt out ... through an opt-out preference signal
universal_opt_out.notes: As codified, § 14-4707(f)(3) is phrased permissively ('may utilize') and disjunctively (link OR signal), so the text does not unambiguously mandate honoring signals; many commentators nonetheless treat signal recognition as required. Signal mechanism conditions (f)(4)-(5): consumer-friendly; clear language; consistent with similar mechanisms; lets controller reasonably determine Maryland residency and legitimacy; requires affirmative, unambiguous, voluntary choice; may not unfairly disadvantage another controller or use a default setting to opt out. § 14-4707(g) addresses conflict between a signal and controller-specific settings ('the controller may notify the consumer of a conflict and provide the choice to confirm'). laws.cure_period: Discretionary: Division MAY issue a notice of violation if cure is possible; if issued, at least 60 days to cure. Applies only to alleged violations occurring on or before 2027-04-01 (§ 14-4714).
laws.enforcer: Division of Consumer Protection, Office of the Maryland Attorney General; violation is an unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practice under Title 13 (§ 14-4713)
laws.private_right_of_action: No private action under the Consumer Protection Act for MODPA violations (§ 14-4713(a)(2) excludes § 13-408); § 14-4713(b): section 'does not prevent a consumer from pursuing any other remedy provided by law'.

universal_opt_out.quote: A controller that recognizes opt-out preference signals that have been approved by other state laws or regulations is in compliance with this subdivision.

universal_opt_out.quote: A controller is not required to comply ... if: ... (d) The controller does not process similar or identical requests ... for the purpose of complying with similar or identical laws or regulations of another state.
universal_opt_out.notes: Conditional duty framed as an authorized-agent designation 'using a technology, including a link to an Internet website, an Internet browser setting or extension, or a global setting on an electronic device'. Covers opt-out of targeted advertising and sale only (§ 87-1107(2)(e)(i)-(ii)). Controller 'shall comply' if it can verify, with commercially reasonable effort, the consumer's identity and the agent's authority; NOT required if (a) request not communicated clearly and unambiguously, (b) cannot verify Nebraska residency with commercially reasonable effort, (c) controller lacks the ability to process the request, or (d) controller does not process similar/identical requests to comply with another state's laws. Technology must not unfairly disadvantage another controller, must not use a default setting, and must be consumer-friendly. No separate delayed date in the statute (operative with the Act). GPC not named.

laws.cure_period: 30-day cure after written AG notice; AG may not sue if violation is cured and written statements are provided. No sunset (§ 87-1122).
laws.enforcer: Nebraska Attorney General (exclusive authority, § 87-1119; civil penalty up to $7,500 per violation, § 87-1124)

required_website_behavior.behavior: Comply with opt-out requests (targeted advertising, sale) sent through a browser setting/extension or global device setting acting as the consumer's authorized agent, subject to the statutory exceptions (notably: not required if the controller does not process similar requests under another state's law).
required_website_behavior.quote: an Internet browser setting or extension, or a global setting on an electronic device
required_website_behavior.applies_when: Covered controller; exceptions in § 87-1111(5)(a)-(d)

required_website_behavior.behavior: Clearly and conspicuously disclose sale of personal data / targeted advertising and how to opt out. (No prescribed link or label.)
required_website_behavior.quote: the controller shall clearly and conspicuously disclose that process and the manner in which a consumer may exercise the right to opt out
required_website_behavior.applies_when: Controller sells personal data to any third party or processes personal data for targeted advertising

required_website_behavior.behavior: Establish two or more secure and reliable methods for consumer requests; if the controller maintains a website, provide a mechanism on the website to submit requests (an online-only controller with a direct relationship need only provide an email address). No new account may be required.
required_website_behavior.quote: the controller shall provide a mechanism on the website for a consumer to submit a request
required_website_behavior.applies_when: Covered controller that maintains a website

required_website_behavior.behavior: Provide a reasonably accessible and clear privacy notice: categories of personal data incl. any sensitive data; purposes; how to exercise rights and appeal; categories shared with third parties; categories of third parties; description of each request method.
required_website_behavior.quote: A controller shall provide each consumer with a reasonably accessible and clear privacy notice
required_website_behavior.applies_when: Covered controller

required_website_behavior.behavior: Obtain consent before processing sensitive data.
required_website_behavior.quote: Process the sensitive data of a consumer without obtaining the consumer's consent
required_website_behavior.applies_when: Covered controller processing sensitive data

required_website_behavior.behavior: Small businesses must not sell sensitive personal data without prior consumer consent.

2026 N.H. Laws ch. 168:1 adds RSA 507-H:6, I(e-1): a controller shall 'Not sell a child's personal data' (reported by secondary sources as HB 1460, signed 2026-06-19).

applicability.summary: Persons that conduct business in NH or produce products/services targeted to NH residents and that during a one-year period met a consumer-count threshold. No revenue threshold. Nonprofits and institutions of higher education are exempt.

thresholds.description: Controlled or processed personal data of not less than 35,000 unique consumers (excluding data processed solely to complete a payment transaction)
Controlled or processed personal data of not less than 10,000 unique consumers AND derived more than 25 percent of gross revenue from sale of personal data

Nonprofit organizations

universal_opt_out.quote: Not later than January 1, 2025, allowing a consumer to opt-out ... through an opt-out preference signal sent, with such consumer's consent
universal_opt_out.notes: Covers targeted advertising and sale. Signal platform/technology must: not unfairly disadvantage another controller; not use a default setting (consumer must make an affirmative, freely given, unambiguous choice); be consumer-friendly; be as consistent as possible with similar mechanisms under federal/state law; enable controller to determine state residency and legitimacy of the request. Signal prevails over conflicting controller-specific setting/loyalty program (controller may notify and offer to confirm). Statute does not name GPC. NH DOJ FAQ pages returned HTTP 403 and could not be checked for GPC recognition.

laws.citation: N.J.S.A. 56:8-166.4 et seq.; P.L. 2023, c. 266 (approved 2024-01-16); amended and supplemented by P.L. 2026, c. 25 (C.56:8-166.20 et al.)

amendments.description: P.L. 2026, c. 25 (A5328), approved 2026-06-30, effective immediately: amends C.56:8-166.12 to add a.(6) 'not sell sensitive data, which shall apply to all individuals or legal entities regardless of the number of consumers whose data the individual or entity controls or processes'; adds data broker / data collector registration (C.56:8-166.20; subsection b. registry inoperative for 270 days after enactment), a ban on data brokers/collectors selling or licensing sensitive data (C.56:8-166.22), and a $50,000-per-record civil penalty (C.56:8-166.23).

applicability.summary: Controllers that conduct business in NJ or produce products/services targeted to NJ residents and that during a calendar year meet a consumer-count threshold. No revenue threshold; the second prong is triggered by ANY revenue or discount from sale of personal data (no percentage). No general nonprofit exemption in the statute. Since 2026-06-30 the sensitive-data sale ban applies regardless of consumer count.

thresholds.description: Control or process personal data of at least 100,000 consumers (excluding data processed solely to complete a payment transaction)
Control or process personal data of at least 25,000 consumers AND the controller derives revenue, or receives a discount on the price of any goods or services, from the sale of personal data
Ban on selling sensitive data applies 'regardless of the number of consumers whose data the individual or entity controls or processes'

key_exemptions: HIPAA PHI
Financial institutions, data or affiliates subject to GLBA Title V
Insurance institutions subject to C.17:23A-1 et seq.
Consumer reporting agency data under FCRA
State agencies and political subdivisions
Human-subjects research data
No entity-level nonprofit or higher-education exemption appears in § 10

laws.sensitive_data_notes: Processing sensitive data requires prior consent (C.56:8-166.12(a)(4)); since 2026-06-30 sale of sensitive data is prohibited outright (C.56:8-166.12(a)(6)), subject to the exemptions in P.L.2026, c.25.

universal_opt_out.quote: shall allow consumers to exercise the right to opt out of such processing through a user-selected universal opt-out mechanism
universal_opt_out.notes: Statute says 'Beginning not later than six months following the effective date' (computed 2025-07-15 from the 2025-01-15 effective date). Applies to controllers processing for targeted advertising or sale. Mechanism must: not permit its manufacturer to unfairly disadvantage another controller; not use a default setting that opts a consumer IN unless the consumer selected it; be consumer-friendly, clearly described, easy to use; be as consistent as possible with similar mechanisms under other law; enable the controller to accurately determine NJ residency and legitimacy. DCA 'may' adopt technical specifications (§ 8.c); none adopted (2025 proposal lapsed). GPC is not named in the statute.

laws.cure_period: 30-day cure after Division notice (if cure deemed possible) required 'until the first day of the 18th month next following the effective date' (computed 2026-07-01); no statutory cure right after that.
laws.enforcer: New Jersey Attorney General (sole and exclusive authority); Division of Consumer Affairs issues notices and rules; violations are unlawful practices under the Consumer Fraud Act (C.56:8-166.17, -166.19)

required_website_behavior.behavior: Allow consumers to opt out of targeted advertising and sale through a user-selected universal opt-out mechanism.
required_website_behavior.quote: shall allow consumers to exercise the right to opt out of such processing through a user-selected universal opt-out mechanism
required_website_behavior.applies_when: Controller processes personal data for targeted advertising or sells personal data

required_website_behavior.behavior: Clearly and conspicuously disclose sale, targeted advertising and significant-decision profiling, and how to opt out. (The statute does not prescribe a specific opt-out link or link label.)
required_website_behavior.quote: the controller shall clearly and conspicuously disclose such sale or processing, as well as the manner in which a consumer may exercise the right to opt out
required_website_behavior.applies_when: Controller sells personal data or processes it for targeted advertising or profiling with legal/similarly significant effects

required_website_behavior.behavior: Provide a reasonably accessible, clear, meaningful privacy notice including: categories of data processed; purposes; categories of third parties to which data may be disclosed; categories of data shared; how to exercise rights incl. contact information and appeal; the process for notifying consumers of material changes plus the notice's effective date; active email/online contact mechanism.
required_website_behavior.quote: the process by which the controller notifies consumers of material changes to the notification ... along with the effective date of the notice
required_website_behavior.applies_when: Covered controller

required_website_behavior.behavior: Obtain consent before processing sensitive data; provide revocation mechanism at least as easy as consent (stop within 15 days).
required_website_behavior.quote: not process sensitive data concerning a consumer without first obtaining the consumer's consent
required_website_behavior.applies_when: Covered controller processing sensitive data

required_website_behavior.behavior: Do not sell sensitive data (applies regardless of consumer-count thresholds).
required_website_behavior.quote: not sell sensitive data, which shall apply to all individuals or legal entities regardless of the number of consumers
required_website_behavior.applies_when: Any individual or legal entity (subject to the act's data/entity exemptions)

required_website_behavior.behavior: Obtain consent before targeted advertising, sale, or significant-decision profiling for consumers known (actual knowledge or wilful disregard) to be 13 to under 17.
required_website_behavior.quote: at least 13 years of age but younger than 17 years of age
required_website_behavior.applies_when: Covered controller with knowledge of age

required_website_behavior.behavior: Do not require a consumer to create a new account to exercise a right.
required_website_behavior.quote: require a consumer to create a new account in order to exercise a right
required_website_behavior.applies_when: Covered controller

Proposal only; not binding.

Secondary sources (Troutman, 2026-06-05) report the proposal expired on 2026-06-02 without adoption under the NJ APA one-year rule and no re-proposal was found. njconsumeraffairs.gov blocks automated fetching (bot-protection page), so neither adoption nor lapse could be confirmed on the official site. Effective date 2025-01-15 (365th day after 2024-01-16 approval), UOOM date 2025-07-15 and cure sunset 2026-07-01 are computed from statutory formulas, not printed as dates in the act; the official DCA FAQ could not be fetched to confirm.
Statute refers to 'user-selected universal opt-out mechanism' without naming GPC; the DCA FAQ (which reportedly discusses mechanisms) could not be fetched.

P.L.2026, c.25 § 1 applies the ban to 'all individuals or legal entities regardless of the number of consumers'; interaction with the definition of 'controller', the c.266 exemptions and the c.25 § 3.b exemptions needs counsel review.

Unlike DE/NH, the NJ statute does not expressly require an opt-out hyperlink; the lapsed proposed rules would have added detail. Record only the 'clearly and conspicuously disclose' duty as statutory.

universal_opt_out.quote: Allow a consumer or authorized agent to send a signal to the controller that indicates the consumer's preference to opt out
universal_opt_out.notes: Signal covers opt-out of sale and targeted advertising (not profiling). The platform/technology must: not unfairly disadvantage another controller; not use a default setting; be consumer friendly; be as consistent as possible with similar mechanisms required under federal or state law; and enable the controller to accurately determine Oregon residency and legitimacy of the request. Statute does not name GPC; the Oregon DOJ FAQ names 'Global Privacy Control' as an example of an opt-out preference signal. Separately, ORS 646A.576(4) (operative 2024-07-01) lets a consumer designate an authorized agent via internet link, browser setting, browser extension or global device setting, and the controller must comply if it can verify identity and authority with commercially reasonable effort.

laws.cure_period: None since 2026-01-01 for most controllers. Before that, 30-day cure after AG notice. Residual 30-day cure for qualifying noncommercial educational broadcast stations repealed 2026-07-01 (Or. Laws 2025 c. 417 §§ 5-6).
laws.enforcer: Oregon Attorney General (exclusive authority, ORS 646A.589(7)). Civil penalty up to $7,500 per violation; 5-year limitation period.

laws.short_name: Texas Data Privacy and Security Act (TDPSA)

amendments.description: Acts 2025, 89th Leg., R.S., ch. 1174 (H.B. 149), Sec. 3 amended § 541.104 (duties of processor), eff. 2026-01-01. It is the only amendment note in the chapter as fetched; no change to §§ 541.002, 541.051, 541.055, 541.101-541.103.

applicability.summary: No revenue or consumer-count threshold. Applies to a person that conducts business in Texas or produces a product or service consumed by Texas residents, processes or sells personal data, and is not a small business as defined by the U.S. Small Business Administration. SBA small businesses are still subject to § 541.107 (consent before selling sensitive data).

thresholds.description: Conducts business in Texas or produces a product/service consumed by Texas residents; processes or engages in the sale of personal data; and is not a small business as defined by the U.S. SBA
Small businesses (SBA definition) may not sell sensitive personal data without prior consumer consent

key_exemptions: Small businesses as defined by the U.S. SBA (except § 541.107)
State agencies and political subdivisions
GLBA financial institutions and data
HIPAA covered entities and business associates
Nonprofit organizations
Institutions of higher education
Electric utilities, power generation companies, retail electric providers
Employment-context data (§ 541.003(15))

universal_opt_out.citation: Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 541.055(e)-(f); H.B. 4 (2023) Sec. 7(b)
universal_opt_out.quote: an Internet browser setting or extension, or a global setting on an electronic device
universal_opt_out.notes: Framed as an authorized-agent designation made through a technology (website link, browser setting/extension, or global device setting) to opt out of targeted advertising and sale (§ 541.051(b)(5)(A)-(B) only; not profiling). Controller 'shall comply' if it can verify with commercially reasonable effort the consumer's identity and the agent's authority. Controller is NOT required to comply if: (1) the request is not communicated clearly and unambiguously; (2) it cannot verify with commercially reasonable effort that the consumer is a Texas resident; (3) it does not possess the ability to process the request; or (4) it does not process similar or identical requests received for the purpose of complying with similar laws of another state. Under § 541.055(f) the technology may not unfairly disadvantage another controller, may not use a default setting, and must be consumer-friendly. 'Global Privacy Control' is not named in the statute. Effective date: the codified section note says 'eff. July 1, 2024', but H.B. 4 Sec. 7(b) states that § 541.055(e) takes effect January 1, 2025.

laws.cure_period: 30 days after written notice; requires written statement that violation was cured, consumer notified, supporting documentation, and policy changes (§ 541.154). No sunset in text.
laws.enforcer: Texas Attorney General (exclusive authority, § 541.151). Civil penalty up to $7,500 per violation (§ 541.155).

regulator_guidance.summary: Texas AG page summarises the Act: effective July 1, 2024; SBA-defined small businesses generally exempt except they must obtain consent before selling sensitive data; controllers must establish two or more request methods; 30-day cure period before enforcement. The page text fetched did not mention global privacy control or opt-out signals.

uncertainty.detail: Whether a given business is a 'small business as defined by the United States Small Business Administration' depends on SBA size standards by industry (NAICS); the statute gives no number.
§ 541.055(e)(4) excuses a controller that does not process similar or identical requests under another state's law; scope of this condition is a legal judgment.
'Sale' includes transfer for 'monetary or other valuable consideration' (§ 541.001(28)), broader than Virginia; application to ad-tech is fact-specific.

laws.citation: Lei n. 13.709, de 14 de agosto de 2018 (Lei Geral de Protecao de Dados Pessoais)

amendments.description: Amended by Lei 13.853/2019 (creating the ANPD and revising arts. 3, 7, 18, 65 among others) and Lei 14.010/2020 (administrative sanctions in arts. 52-54 effective 2021-08-01, art. 65 I-A).

applicability.summary: Art. 3: applies to any processing operation by a natural or legal person, regardless of the country of its seat or where the data are located, if (I) the processing is carried out in Brazil, (II) the processing aims at offering or supplying goods or services to, or processing data of, individuals located in Brazil, or (III) the personal data were collected in Brazil (data are deemed collected in Brazil if the data subject was there at the time of collection, art. 3 s. 1). No revenue or volume threshold. LGPD has no cookie-specific rule: processing needs one of the art. 7 legal bases (consent, legitimate interest, contract, legal obligation, etc.). Consent is therefore not always required; it is one basis.

thresholds.description: Extraterritorial: offering goods/services to, or processing data of, individuals in Brazil; or data collected in Brazil.

key_exemptions: Art. 4 exclusions (personal/non-economic, journalistic, artistic, academic, public security) - art. 4 not read in this session
ANPD small-processing-agent regulation (Resolucao CD/ANPD n. 2/2022) eases some duties - not fetched

universal_opt_out.quote: O consentimento pode ser revogado a qualquer momento mediante manifestacao expressa do titular, por procedimento gratuito e facilitado
universal_opt_out.notes: LGPD is silent on browser signals/GPC. Art. 18 s. 2 gives a right to object to processing based on a non-consent basis 'em caso de descumprimento ao disposto nesta Lei' (i.e. only in case of non-compliance). The ANPD cookie guide passages read do not name GPC. (Quote reproduced without diacritics.)

laws.cure_period: None fixed; a warning with a deadline for corrective measures is one available sanction (art. 52, I).
laws.enforcer: Autoridade Nacional de Protecao de Dados (ANPD). Simple fine up to 2% of the legal entity's/group's revenue in Brazil in the last fiscal year, capped at BRL 50,000,000 per infraction (art. 52, II).
laws.private_right_of_action: Yes in principle (arts. 22 and 42 on individual/collective judicial protection and liability) - not read in this session.

required_website_behavior.behavior: Process personal data (including via cookies/trackers) only under one of the art. 7 legal bases, e.g. the data subject's consent or the controller's legitimate interest where the data subject's fundamental rights do not prevail.
required_website_behavior.citation: LGPD art. 7, caput, I and IX
required_website_behavior.quote: O tratamento de dados pessoais somente podera ser realizado nas seguintes hipoteses
required_website_behavior.applies_when: LGPD applies under art. 3 and cookies/trackers process personal data

required_website_behavior.behavior: Where consent is the basis, it must be a free, informed and unambiguous manifestation for a specific purpose; generic authorisations are void; the controller bears the burden of proving valid consent.
required_website_behavior.citation: LGPD art. 5, XII; art. 8, ss. 2 and 4
required_website_behavior.quote: manifestacao livre, informada e inequivoca pela qual o titular concorda com o tratamento de seus dados pessoais para uma finalidade determinada
required_website_behavior.applies_when: Controller relies on consent

required_website_behavior.behavior: Allow consent to be revoked at any time through a free and facilitated procedure.
required_website_behavior.quote: por procedimento gratuito e facilitado
required_website_behavior.applies_when: Controller relies on consent

required_website_behavior.behavior: Make available clear, adequate and conspicuous information about the processing: specific purpose, form and duration, controller identity and contact details, shared use and its purpose, responsibilities of the agents, and data subject rights with explicit mention of art. 18.
required_website_behavior.quote: deverao ser disponibilizadas de forma clara, adequada e ostensiva
required_website_behavior.applies_when: LGPD applies

required_website_behavior.behavior: Sensitive personal data processed on the basis of consent requires specific and highlighted consent for specific purposes; children's data requires specific, highlighted consent from a parent or legal guardian.
required_website_behavior.quote: consentir, de forma especifica e destacada, para finalidades especificas
required_website_behavior.applies_when: Site processes sensitive data or children's data

regulator_guidance.summary: ANPD 'Guia Orientativo - Cookies e protecao de dados pessoais' (v1.0, October 2022) - NON-BINDING orientation guide, not a regulation. Consent is not appropriate for strictly necessary cookies (legitimate interest or another basis may apply); legitimate interest will 'dificilmente' be the most appropriate basis for advertising cookies, especially third-party cookies, behavioural profiling or cross-site tracking - consent is considered more appropriate there.

ANPD guide, banner good practices (described as non-exhaustive 'boas praticas'): provide an easily visible button to reject all non-necessary cookies on first- and second-level banners; allow consent per specific purpose; keep consent-based cookies disabled by default; provide an easy way to revoke; avoid making reject buttons hard to see and avoid tacit consent mechanisms (e.g. 'by continuing to browse you agree').

amendments.description: s. 6.1 (valid consent) added by the Digital Privacy Act, S.C. 2015, c. 32 (date from memory). Justice Laws shows the Act as last amended 2025-03-04 (nature of that amendment not examined).

applicability.summary: Applies to personal information an organization collects, uses or discloses in the course of commercial activities (s. 4(1)). No revenue or volume threshold. Organizations subject to provincial laws declared substantially similar (Quebec, Alberta, British Columbia) are exempt for intra-provincial activity under orders made under s. 26(2)(b). regulator_guidance.summary: OPC Guidelines on privacy and online behavioural advertising: opt-out consent for OBA 'could be considered reasonable' if individuals are made aware of the purposes clearly at or before collection (not buried in a privacy policy), are told the parties involved, can easily opt out, the opt-out takes effect immediately and is persistent, information is limited to non-sensitive information as far as practicable, and is destroyed or de-identified as soon as possible.

OPC OBA guidelines: do not use for OBA technologies that individuals cannot decline or that make the service unusable if declined (zombie cookies, supercookies, device fingerprinting); as a best practice avoid tracking children and tracking on sites aimed at children; avoid sensitive information (health, financial, etc.) - express opt-in consent generally expected for sensitive information.

uncertainty.detail: PIPEDA does not mention cookies. applicability.summary: Applies to personal information that a person collects, holds, uses or communicates to third persons in the course of carrying on an enterprise within the meaning of art. 1525 of the Civil Code (s. 1). No revenue or volume threshold. The Act has no express territorial clause; application to an out-of-province or U.S. enterprise collecting information from people in Quebec is generally asserted by the CAI but was not verified from a primary source in this session.

thresholds.description: Any enterprise (Civil Code art. 1525); no size threshold.

key_exemptions: s. 9.1 privacy-by-default does not apply to privacy settings for browser cookies (s. 9.1 para 2)

universal_opt_out.quote: must first inform the person (1) of the use of such technology; and (2) of the means available to activate the functions
universal_opt_out.notes: The Act is silent on browser signals/GPC. required_website_behavior.quote: must, when the information is collected and subsequently on request, inform that person

required_website_behavior.behavior: Publish on the enterprise's website a confidentiality policy drafted in clear and simple language, and give notice of amendments to it.
required_website_behavior.quote: must publish on the enterprise's website, if applicable, a confidentiality policy drafted in clear and simple language
required_website_behavior.applies_when: Enterprise collects personal information through technological means

required_website_behavior.behavior: Consent must be clear, free and informed, given for specific purposes, requested for each purpose in clear and simple language, and (if requested in writing) presented separately from other information; express consent is required for sensitive personal information; minors under 14 need parental/tutor consent.
required_website_behavior.quote: Consent under this Act must be clear, free and informed and be given for specific purposes.
required_website_behavior.applies_when: Enterprise relies on consent

required_website_behavior.behavior: For a technological product or service offered to the public that has privacy settings, set them to the highest level of confidentiality by default. This does NOT apply to privacy settings for browser cookies.

required_website_behavior.applies_when: Enterprise offers a technological product/service with privacy settings

regulator_guidance.summary: CAI (Loi 25 summary page): organisations must inform people in advance of the use of identification, location or profiling technologies, and 'ces technologies ne pourront etre activees par defaut'.

CAI consent page / Lignes directrices 2023-1 (final version published 2023-10-31 per secondary sources): eight validity criteria - consent must be manifest, free, informed, specific, granular, understandable, temporary and requested separately; express consent for sensitive information. The CAI page states its texts are simplified explanations and the law prevails.

applicability.summary: Art. 3(1): applies to circumstances that have an effect in Switzerland, even if initiated abroad - so a foreign website processing personal data of people in Switzerland can be covered. No size threshold. Private processing does not need a legal basis by default: it needs justification (consent, overriding private/public interest, or law - art. 31(1)) only where it breaches personality rights, e.g. processing contrary to the art. 6 principles or contrary to the data subject's express wishes (art. 30(2)). Art. 14 requires a Swiss representative for foreign controllers only where processing is connected with offering goods/services or monitoring behaviour in Switzerland AND is large-scale, regular and high-risk.

thresholds.description: Effects doctrine: circumstances having an effect in Switzerland even if initiated abroad.

required_website_behavior.applies_when: FADP applies

regulator_guidance.summary: FDPIC cookie guidelines (v1.0 2025-01-22; v1.1 2025-10-06): 'Neither the FADP nor Article 45c TCA require that consent be obtained in order for data processing via non-essential cookies to be lawful' - consent is one of several justifications. But an opt-out (right to reject) is 'mandatory' for non-essential cookies under art. 45c TCA.

FDPIC: non-essential cookie use involving sensitive personal data or resulting in high-risk profiling is a severe intrusion; controllers cannot rely on overriding private interest or a mere opt-out and 'must obtain express consent ... before carrying out the processing' (section 3.10.1). v1.1 adds that giving third parties paid access to visitor data via embedded third-party cookies across several sites may amount to high-risk profiling requiring consent, and adds material on location data and cookie paywalls.
FDPIC published a public-facing cookies factsheet on 2026-03-31 as a follow-up to the guidelines, and announced awareness work followed by supervisory measures based on the guidelines.

uncertainty.detail: Statute is opt-out (art. 45c) plus FADP justification rules. When tracking amounts to 'high-risk profiling' (FADP art. 5 let. g) and so needs explicit consent is a case-by-case judgement; the FDPIC's view that third-party advertising tracking across sites can cross that line is guidance, not statute. A site serving both EU and Swiss visitors with an EU-style opt-in banner would exceed the Swiss statutory minimum.
Fedlex English texts are unofficial translations without legal force; German/French/Italian texts govern. Art. 7(3) quote was truncated in extraction.

The TCA text read is the 1 Sept 2023 consolidation; later consolidations could not be retrieved, so amendments to art. 45c after that date cannot be excluded (the FDPIC guidelines of Oct 2025 still describe art. 45c in the same terms).

laws.citation: Directive 2002/58/EC, art. 5(3), as amended by Directive 2009/136/EC

amendments.description: Directive 2009/136/EC replaced art. 5(3): moved from information-plus-right-to-refuse to prior consent with clear and comprehensive information.

applicability.summary: A directive: binds Member States, which implement art. 5(3) in national law enforced by national authorities. Applies to storing information, or gaining access to information already stored, in the terminal equipment of a subscriber or user in the Union, whether or not the information is personal data (Planet49, ruling 2). The directive has no size, revenue or establishment threshold; whether and how a non-EU website operator is reached depends on each Member State's implementing law (not researched). Where personal data is involved GDPR art. 3(2) separately reaches non-EU controllers that offer goods/services to, or monitor the behaviour of, people in the Union.

thresholds.description: No threshold. Two exemptions only: (1) sole purpose of carrying out transmission of a communication; (2) strictly necessary to provide an information society service explicitly requested by the user.

key_exemptions: Technical storage/access for the sole purpose of carrying out the transmission of a communication
Storage/access strictly necessary to provide an information society service explicitly requested by the subscriber or user

universal_opt_out.notes: Art. 5(3) text read in this session does not mention browser signals or GPC. It requires prior consent, so the default with no signal is already 'no non-exempt storage/access'. Recital 66 of 2009/136/EC (consent via browser settings 'where technically possible and effective') is known from memory but was not in the consolidated text read (consolidations omit recitals) - not verified.

laws.cure_period: None in the directive; national law governs.
laws.enforcer: National authorities designated by each Member State (data protection authority and/or telecom regulator, varies by Member State).
laws.private_right_of_action: Art. 13(6)/15(2) leave remedies to national law and cross-refer to the data protection rules; depends on Member State law (not researched).

applicability.summary: Applies to processing in the context of an EU establishment, and (art. 3(2)) to non-EU controllers/processors processing personal data of data subjects who are in the Union where the processing relates to (a) offering goods or services to them or (b) monitoring their behaviour within the Union. No revenue or volume threshold. A U.S. site that merely happens to be accessible from the EU is not automatically covered; 'offering' and 'monitoring' are fact-specific (see recitals 23-24, not quoted here). Art. 27 requires a non-EU controller caught by art. 3(2) to designate an EU representative, with an exception for occasional low-risk processing.

thresholds.description: Extraterritorial reach: offering goods/services to, or monitoring behaviour of, data subjects in the Union.

key_exemptions: Purely personal or household activity (art. 2(2)(c), not quoted)

It does not name GPC or Do Not Track, and nothing read in this session (statute, Planet49, EDPB 05/2020, EDPB 2/2023) states that controllers must treat a GPC header as a valid objection or as a refusal/withdrawal of consent. Recorded as unclear, not as 'no'. The 'targeted_advertising: true' and 'profiling: true' flags above reflect the art. 21(2)-(3) right to object to direct marketing (incl. related profiling), which was not separately quoted in this session; GDPR has no 'sale' concept.

laws.cure_period: None.

laws.private_right_of_action: Yes in principle - arts. 79 and 82 (judicial remedy and compensation); not quoted in this session.

required_website_behavior.behavior: Do not store information (cookies, local storage, etc.) or read information from a visitor's device before the visitor has consented, unless the storage/access is solely for transmitting a communication or strictly necessary for a service the visitor explicitly requested. This is the rule Member States must implement; the binding text for any given site is the national implementing law.
required_website_behavior.quote: only allowed on condition that the subscriber or user concerned has given his or her consent, having been provided with clear and comprehensive information
required_website_behavior.applies_when: Site stores or accesses non-exempt information on devices of users in an EU Member State (subject to that Member State's implementing law)

required_website_behavior.behavior: Consent for cookies cannot be obtained with a pre-checked checkbox that the user must deselect; it requires an active indication.
required_website_behavior.citation: CJEU C-673/17 Planet49, operative part 1 (interpreting Directive 2002/58/EC arts. 2(f), 5(3) and GDPR arts. 4(11), 6(1)(a))
required_website_behavior.quote: consent ... is not validly constituted if ... permitted by way of a pre-checked checkbox which the user must deselect to refuse
required_website_behavior.applies_when: Any consent request for storage/access under art. 5(3)

required_website_behavior.quote: not to be interpreted differently according to whether or not the information stored or accessed ... is personal data
required_website_behavior.applies_when: Any non-exempt storage/access

required_website_behavior.quote: includes the duration of the operation of cookies and whether or not third parties may have access to those cookies
required_website_behavior.applies_when: Any consent request for cookies

required_website_behavior.applies_when: Processing (or art. 5(3) storage/access) relies on consent

required_website_behavior.applies_when: Processing relies on consent

required_website_behavior.behavior: Provide privacy information at the time personal data is collected: controller identity and contact details, purposes and legal basis, recipients, third-country transfers, retention period, data subject rights including withdrawal of consent, and the right to complain to a supervisory authority.
required_website_behavior.citation: GDPR art. 13(1)-(2) (and art. 12 on form, art. 14 for data not obtained from the data subject - arts. 12 and 14 not quoted in this session)
required_website_behavior.quote: the controller shall, at the time when personal data are obtained, provide the data subject with all of the following information
required_website_behavior.applies_when: GDPR applies under art. 3 and the site collects personal data

regulator_guidance.summary: EDPB Guidelines 05/2020 (v1.1, adopted 4 May 2020), para 39: access to services and functionalities must not be made conditional on consent to storage/access on the user's device ('cookie walls'); paras 40-41 give the example of a content-blocking 'Accept cookies' overlay as not valid consent.
EDPB Guidelines 05/2020, para 86: scrolling or swiping through a webpage or similar user activity 'will not under any circumstances' satisfy the requirement of a clear and affirmative action.

EDPB Guidelines 2/2023 on the technical scope of art. 5(3) (v2.0, adopted 7 October 2024, final after consultation): treats URL and pixel tracking, local processing, tracking based on IP only, intermittent/mediated IoT reporting and unique identifiers as use cases potentially within art. 5(3) - i.e. the rule is not limited to cookies. Para 51 addresses tracking information added to URLs or pixels.

uncertainty.detail: Art. 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive is implemented by national law and enforced by national authorities whose guidance differs (e.g. France's CNIL guidelines/recommendation on cookies and analytics exemption; Germany's TDDDG s. 25 and DSK guidance; Italy's Garante 2021 guidelines; Spain's AEPD guide). None of the 27 national regimes was researched. Points that vary nationally include: whether a 'reject all' button on the first layer is required, analytics exemptions, consent lifetime / re-prompt interval, cookie walls / pay-or-consent, and fine levels.

GDPR art. 21(5) permits objection 'by automated means using technical specifications' but no EU-level source read here names GPC or requires honoring it. Some national authorities or courts may have taken positions (not researched). Do not represent GPC as legally required in the EU; do not represent it as legally irrelevant either.

A first-layer 'reject all' button is NOT stated in the ePrivacy Directive or GDPR text. It derives from regulator positions (EDPB Cookie Banner Taskforce report of January 2023 and national authorities) which were not fetched in this session. Treat as regulator expectation, not statutory text.

uncertainty.detail: 2011-05-25 (transposition deadline of Directive 2009/136/EC) is from researcher memory; the consolidated text read shows the amended wording but not the transposition deadline. Actual national commencement dates differ.

Whether a U.S. agency client site is 'offering goods or services' to or 'monitoring' people in the Union under GDPR art. 3(2) is fact-specific (language, currency, targeting, use of behavioural tracking). EDPB Guidelines 3/2018 on territorial scope were not fetched.

These provisions were in the fetched document but only arts. 3, 4(11), 7, 13, 21(5), 27, 83(5) and 99 were extracted and read verbatim. Statements about the others rely on researcher knowledge of the same text.

laws.citation: Privacy and Electronic Communications (EC Directive) Regulations 2003 (SI 2003/2426), reg. 6 and Sch. A1, as substituted/inserted by Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 s. 112 and Sch. 12

amendments.description: Reg. 6 substituted and new Schedule A1 (exceptions) inserted by DUAA 2025 s. 112 and Sch. 12; in force 2026-02-05 (SI 2026/82 reg. 2(w), 2(z13)). New consent-free exceptions, each with conditions: statistical purposes about how the service is used (Sch. A1 para 5), website appearance/functionality preferences (para 6), emergency assistance location (para 7); plus transmission (para 3) and strictly necessary incl. security/fraud examples (para 4). Paras 5 and 6 require clear and comprehensive information and a simple, free means of objecting.

PECR enforcement regime replaced: DUAA s. 115 and Sch. 13 substitute PECR Sch. 1 so that DPA 2018 Parts 5-7 enforcement powers (incl. penalty notices) apply to PECR. As modified, DPA 2018 s. 157(2)(a) lists reg. 6 among provisions attracting the 'higher maximum amount' - GBP 17,500,000 or, for an undertaking, 4% of total annual worldwide turnover if higher (s. 157(5)). Previously the PECR maximum was GBP 500,000 (prior figure from memory, not fetched). In force 2026-02-05 (SI 2026/82 reg. 2(y), 2(z14), with transitional regs 8-11).
Reg. 6A gives the Secretary of State power to add further exceptions by statutory instrument after consulting the Information Commissioner.

applicability.summary: Applies to any 'person' who stores information, or gains access to information stored, in the terminal equipment of a subscriber or user - including instigating it, and including collecting or monitoring information automatically emitted by the device (reg. 6(2)). No size threshold; applies whether or not the information is personal data. PECR itself has no express extraterritorial clause in the provisions read; how it applies to a website operator with no UK presence was not established from a primary source. UK GDPR art. 3(2) separately reaches non-UK controllers offering goods/services to, or monitoring the behaviour of, data subjects in the UK.

thresholds.description: No threshold. Prohibition subject to the Schedule A1 exceptions.

key_exemptions: Sch. A1 para 3: sole purpose of transmitting a communication
Sch. A1 para 4: strictly necessary for an information society service requested by the user (incl. security examples)

Sch. A1 para 5: statistical purposes about how the service is used, with a view to improving it - only with clear information and a simple free means of objecting, and no onward sharing except to assist with improvements
Sch. A1 para 6: adapting website appearance/functionality to user preferences - only with clear information and a simple free means of objecting
Sch. A1 para 7: locating the user after an emergency-assistance request

universal_opt_out.citation: PECR Sch. A1 para 2(3); ICO storage and access technologies guidance
universal_opt_out.notes: Sch. A1 para 2(3) allows consent to be signified by browser settings or another application. Neither PECR nor the ICO guidance read here names GPC or requires honoring it. ICO guidance says organisations 'must not rely solely on browser settings to indicate consent' and must not rely solely on browser settings as an indication that a person does not object. Non-exempt storage requires prior opt-in anyway, so absence of consent already means no non-exempt storage.

laws.cure_period: None in statute.
laws.enforcer: Information Commissioner (ICO). From 2026-02-05 penalty notices up to GBP 17,500,000 or 4% of worldwide annual turnover for reg. 6 (DPA 2018 s. 157 as applied by PECR Sch. 1 para 18).
laws.private_right_of_action: PECR reg. 30 (compensation for damage) - known from memory, not fetched.

amendments.description: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 made further amendments to UK GDPR/DPA 2018 (e.g. recognised legitimate interests, complaints handling) commenced in stages; those not specific to website cookie behaviour were not researched.

applicability.summary: Art. 3(1): processing in the context of a UK establishment. Art. 3(2): controllers/processors not established in the UK processing personal data of data subjects in the UK where related to offering them goods/services or monitoring their behaviour in the UK. No size threshold. PECR 'consent' has the UK GDPR meaning (PECR reg. 2(1)).

required_website_behavior.behavior: Do not store or access information on a user's device (cookies, pixels, fingerprinting, local storage and similar) unless a Schedule A1 exception applies; the general exception is that the user has been given clear and comprehensive information about the purpose and has consented.
required_website_behavior.quote: Subject to Schedule A1, a person must not store information, or gain access to information stored, in the terminal equipment of a subscriber or user.
required_website_behavior.applies_when: Any storage/access on devices of UK users not within Sch. A1 paras 3-7 (advertising never falls within those exceptions per ICO)

required_website_behavior.behavior: Consent under PECR must meet the UK GDPR standard of consent.
required_website_behavior.quote: "consent" by a user or subscriber corresponds to the data subject's consent in the UK GDPR
required_website_behavior.applies_when: Relying on consent under Sch. A1 para 2

required_website_behavior.behavior: If relying on the statistical-purposes or appearance/functionality exception instead of consent, give users clear and comprehensive information about the purpose and a simple, free means of objecting to the storage or access, and honour objections.
required_website_behavior.quote: a simple means of objecting, free of charge
required_website_behavior.applies_when: Site uses analytics or preference storage for UK users without consent under Sch. A1 para 5 or 6

required_website_behavior.behavior: Information collected under the statistical-purposes exception must be used solely for statistics about how the service is used and must not be shared with others except to help improve the service.
required_website_behavior.quote: collect information for statistical purposes about how the service is used
required_website_behavior.applies_when: Relying on Sch. A1 para 5 (analytics without consent)

regulator_guidance.summary: ICO 'Guidance on the use of storage and access technologies': published as a draft 2024-12-20, updated 2025-07-07 for DUAA changes (exceptions chapter), and FINALISED on 2026-04-29. It is the current ICO guidance replacing the earlier 'cookies and similar technologies' guidance.

ICO: where no exception applies 'you must obtain prior consent'; consent requires a positive opt-in action, silence or inactivity does not qualify; users must be able to withdraw 'with the same ease that they gave it'; the consent mechanism is expected to make it as easy to refuse as to accept (accept-only designs shown as bad practice); non-exempt toggles off by default (good practice).

ICO: 'Online advertising purposes are not exempt from PECR's consent requirements and never have been' - includes frequency capping, ad measurement, click-fraud detection and ad-related fingerprinting. The statistical exception covers aggregate analytics to improve the service; a third-party analytics provider may be used only if it merely assists (acts as processor) and users are told; building audience segments for targeting is outside the exception.

ICO on browser signals: PECR allows browser controls as a way to signify consent, but 'you must not rely solely on browser settings to indicate consent' and must not rely solely on browser settings as an indication that a person does not object.

uncertainty.topic: Territorial scope of PECR for non-UK operators
uncertainty.detail: No express territorial provision of PECR was located/fetched. Whether reg. 6 is enforceable against a U.S. operator with no UK establishment is unsettled in the sources read; UK GDPR art. 3(2) is clearer but covers only personal data processing.

uncertainty.topic: Which penalty tier applies to reg. 6
uncertainty.detail: Conclusion that reg. 6 attracts the 'higher maximum amount' is derived by reading PECR Sch. 1 para 18 (substituting the list in DPA 2018 s. 157(2)(a) with a list including regulation 6) together with unmodified s. 157(2)(a) ('..., the higher maximum amount') and s. 157(5). Each piece was fetched; the combined modified text is not printed on any single page. Transitional regs 8-11 of SI 2026/82 (conduct before 2026-02-05) were not read.

Whether a particular analytics product (e.g. default Google Analytics 4 with Google signals/ads linking) fits Sch. A1 para 5 is not answered by statute; ICO says the provider must act only as processor and data must not be used for other purposes. Tool-specific assessment needed.

'As easy to refuse as accept' is ICO guidance/expectation, not text of reg. 6 or Sch. A1. Cookie walls / consent-or-pay were not covered on the ICO pages fetched (ICO has separate consent-or-pay guidance, not fetched).
